subtopics.title: Rivers That Ignore the Rock — Superimposed and Antecedent Drainage

questions.question: Superimposed drainage forms when a river:
options: Follows the folds of the rock beneath it
Develops on a young cover of rock and is let down onto an older buried structure, keeping its inherited course
Is captured by a stronger neighbour

questions.question: Antecedent drainage forms when:
options: The river is younger than the mountains it crosses
The river predates the structure and cuts down as fast as the land rises across its path
Two rivers merge at a watershed

questions.question: The field evidence shared by both special patterns is:
options: A river crossing a mountain range through a deep gorge instead of flowing around it
A dendritic pattern on uniform rock

questions.question: The one-line memory pair for the two patterns is:
options: Stolen from a neighbour, or lost to the sea
Younger than rain, older than rock
Printed from above, or older than the hills

subtopics.title: Why Catchments Matter — and Why They Are Poorly Managed

questions.question: A drainage basin is:
options: The channel of the main river only
The high ground between two rivers
All the land drained by a river and its tributaries
The dam at the river's end

questions.question: The master principle of catchment management is that:
options: Everything that happens anywhere in the catchment eventually reaches the river
Only riverside activities affect water quality

questions.question: A healthy catchment regulates floods because:
options: Its wetlands and vegetated slopes absorb storms like a sponge and release water slowly

questions.question: Fragmented responsibility causes poor catchment management because:
options: A basin ignores political boundaries, but each authority manages only its own patch, so no one owns the whole system
There are too many catchment agencies
Basins are too small to manage

subtopics.title: Four Human Impacts — Pollution, Overgrazing, Deforestation, Settlement

questions.question: The correct order of the eutrophication chain is:
options: Nutrients in, algal bloom, light blocked, algae die and rot, oxygen crash, aquatic life suffocates
Silt in, water warms, fish leave

questions.question: The standing South African example of a eutrophied dam is:
options: Hartbeespoort Dam, pea-green under algal blooms and hyacinth mats

questions.question: Overgrazing damages rivers because bare, crusted soil:
options: Sheds rapid runoff that strips topsoil, silting rivers and dams and carving dongas

questions.question: Invasive alien trees along South African watercourses are a special problem because they:
options: Consume far more water than the indigenous vegetation they replaced, stealing streamflow
Provide too much shade for fish

subtopics.title: Management Strategies and the Working for Water Case Study

questions.question: Under the National Water Act, catchments are meant to be managed by:
options: Catchment management agencies running whole water management areas with all users at the table

questions.question: Mountain catchments like the Boland and Drakensberg are called water factories because they:
options: Deliver a huge share of national runoff from a tiny share of the land

questions.question: The problem attacked by the Working for Water programme since 1995 is:
options: Invasive alien plants infesting catchments and riverbanks, guzzling water and fuelling fiercer fires

questions.question: Working for Water's famous double dividend is:
options: Measured streamflow returned to rivers, plus tens of thousands of jobs for poor rural communities

questions.question: In the funnel picture, the watershed is:
options: The spout where the river leaves
The rim — the high ground where a raindrop must choose which river to join

questions.question: The most important sentence of the lesson is:
options: Whatever happens anywhere in the funnel ends up in the river

questions.question: Johannesburg's drinking water comes from:
options: A giant borehole under the city
The Vaal's catchment and, via tunnels, Lesotho's mountains

questions.question: The two gorge histories in one line are:
options: Printed from above — superimposed; older than the hills — antecedent
Older than the hills — superimposed; printed from above — antecedent

subtopics.title: The Fish Tank That Turned Green

questions.question: In the fish-tank story, the fish food stands for:
options: Nutrients — nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers, sewage and detergents

questions.question: The six beats of eutrophication, in order, are:
options: Rot, feed, bloom, dark, die, suffocate
Feed, dark, bloom, suffocate, die, rot
Feed, bloom, dark, die, rot, suffocate
Bloom, feed, rot, dark, suffocate, die

questions.question: The fish ultimately die in a eutrophied dam because:
options: The algae poison them directly in all cases
Decomposition of the dead bloom consumes the dissolved oxygen they breathe

questions.question: The sealed city makes floods flashier because:
options: Tar and roofs cannot absorb rain, so storm water reaches the river in minutes
City rain is heavier than farm rain

subtopics.title: Saws, Sponges and the Water Factories

questions.question: Wetlands are called the sponges of the catchment because they:
options: Filter dirt, swallow floods and release water slowly through dry months

questions.question: A vegetated strip kept along a river protects it by:
options: Acting as a living filter that traps farm chemicals and sediment before they reach the water

questions.question: A valley full of wattle is described as a valley drinking its own river because:
options: The invasive trees consume far more water than indigenous fynbos, reducing streamflow

questions.question: The five-sentence case-study answer for Working for Water covers:
options: The name, the date since 1995, the thirsty alien-plant problem, the clearing method, and the double dividend of water plus jobs
The dam heights, the pipe lengths and the budget
The names of all the river systems cleared
The rainfall statistics of each province
